items.title: Rule Change: support "object spread" boolean context

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: This change enhances an existing feature of ESLint

items.body:
### What rule do you want to change?

no-extra-boolean-cast

### What change do you want to make?

Generate more warnings

### How do you think the change should be implemented?

Other

### Example code

```js
Boolean(a ?? !!x)            // ✅ flagged  — "Redundant double negation"
const o = { ...(!!x && a) }  // ❌ not flagged — but the !! is just as redundant
```

### What does the rule currently do for this code?

When `enforceForInnerExpressions` is `true`, it checks the RHS of `??` and correctly determines that the `!!` is unnecessary, and reports on line 1, but it does NOT check the LHS of `&&`.

### What will the rule do after it's changed?

When `enforceForInnerExpressions` is `true`, it will also check the LHS of a `&&` inside an object spread, as a "boolean context".

items.title: Change Request: Expose the active language ID to rules

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: This change enhances an existing feature of ESLint

labels.name: core
labels.description: Relates to ESLint's core APIs and features

items.body:
### ESLint version

v10.9.1

### What problem do you want to solve?

Rules can declare `meta.languages` but the active language ID is not available through the rule context.

For example, `json/json`, `json/jsonc`, and `json/json5` normally have identical `context.languageOptions` and use the same `SourceCode` implementation. A rule therfore cannot reliably determine which JSON language is active.

The filename extension cannot identify the language reliably. Flat config can assign any language to any filename pattern, files can be linted from stdin using a virtual filename, processors can create virtual files, and `.json` files may intentionally use JSONC or JSON5. The configured language is the source of truth, not the filename.

This matters when behavior differs by language. An autofix may emit `\v` or `\0` for JSON5, but those escapes are invalid in JSON and JSONC. Today, a rule must guess from the filename, require a redundant option, or omit otherwise valid behaviour.


### What do you think is the correct solution?

Expose the active runtime language identifier as a read-only rule context property:

```js
context.languageId === 'json/json5'
```

This should use the same normalized identifier semantics as `meta.languages`, ideally using the plugin's `meta.namespace` so configuring a plugin under an alias does not change rule behavior.

A string identifier is preferable to exposing the resolved language object. This information should not be added to `languageOptions` because it describes ESLint's execution context rather than parser or language configuration.

items.title: Bug: new-cap doesn't report names starting with an astral letter

labels.name: accepted
labels.description: There is consensus among the team that this change meets the criteria for inclusion

items.body:
**This issue was created with AI (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5).**

### Environment

Node version: v25.2.1
npm version: v11.6.2
Local ESLint version: v10.11.0 (Currently used)
Global ESLint version: Not found
Operating System: win32 10.0.26200

### What parser are you using?

Default (Espree)

### What did you do?

```js
/*eslint new-cap: "error"*/

new φ(); // reported
new 𐐨(); // not reported

Φ(); // reported
𐐀(); // not reported
```

`𐐨` and `𐐀` are Deseret letters (U+10428, U+10400), so each one is a surrogate pair.

### What did you expect to happen?

All four calls should be reported.

### What actually happened?

```
  3:5  error  A constructor name should not start with a lowercase letter                                    new-cap
  6:1  error  A function with a name starting with an uppercase letter should only be used as a constructor  new-cap

✖ 2 problems (2 errors, 0 warnings)
```

### Link to Minimal Reproducible Example

https://eslint.org/play/#

### Participation

- [x] I am willing to submit a pull request for this issue.

### AI acknowledgment

- [ ] I did not use AI to generate this issue report.
- [x] (If the above is not checked) I have reviewed the AI-generated content before submitting.

### Additional comments

`getCap()` uses `str.charAt(0)`, which returns only the high surrogate (`\uD801`) for these names, so they end up as `"non-alpha"`:

https://github.com/eslint/eslint/blob/39d79ba9650542ac66d585d1899304abd630c07d/lib/rules/new-cap.js#L141-L155

`const [firstChar] = str;` would fix it.

items.title: Change Request: Cache normalized config globals across files to improve performance

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: This change enhances an existing feature of ESLint

labels.name: core
labels.description: Relates to ESLint's core APIs and features

labels.name: accepted
labels.description: There is consensus among the team that this change meets the criteria for inclusion

items.body:
### ESLint version

v10.10.0 (also present on main)

### What problem do you want to solve?

I've been profiling lint times on a larger internal Vue + TypeScript app (~1,000 files, ~1,270 configured globals), and a surprising amount of each run was going into globals handling rather than into rules. Digging in, configured globals get merged and normalized again for every file, and then `no-redeclare` walks every one of them again, per file.

In more detail: `SourceCode#applyLanguageOptions` builds a null-prototype object from the ES, sourceType and configured globals and runs `normalizeConfigGlobal` on each entry, for every file. `addDeclaredGlobals` then copies that object and re-filters the enabled names. But files that match the same configs already share one `languageOptions` object (config-array caches the finalized config per matching set), so the answer is the same every time.

`no-redeclare` (in `eslint:recommended`) then runs its `iterateDeclarations` generator and a rest destructure for every variable in the global scope. That includes every configured global, even though a variable with fewer than two possible declarations can never be reported.

On our app the globals handling alone went from ~1.5s to ~0.5s per lint. To make sure it wasn't just our setup, I reproduced it on ESLint's own `lib/` + `tests/lib/` (742 files) with `@eslint/js` recommended plus `globals.browser` (1,169 globals), 3 runs each:

| | main | proposed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| globals handling (`applyLanguageOptions` + `finalize`) | 1,108–1,149ms | 203–252ms |
| `no-redeclare` | 161–200ms | 17–24ms |
| total lint | 6.86–6.98s | 5.53–5.96s |

So for a pretty ordinary browser project that's roughly 15-20% of the whole lint. With only the built-in ES globals the saving is small (~0.1s), so it mostly helps anyone spreading `globals.browser` or similar. Reported problems were identical in every run.

I also found #16302, which looked at the same per-file merge and switched it to `Object.assign`. That helped, but the work still repeats for every file.

### What do you think is the correct solution?

Two small, independent changes:

1. In `applyLanguageOptions`, cache the merged and normalized globals in a `WeakMap` keyed on the `languageOptions` object. When a file has no inline `/* global */` comments, `addDeclaredGlobals` reuses a cached list of enabled names instead of copying and filtering again. Files with inline globals keep the existing path, and the cached object is never mutated.
2. In `no-redeclare`, skip variables that can't have two declarations (counting identifiers, inline global comments and, with `builtinGlobals`, the configured-global flag) before starting the generator. The count can only overstate what the generator yields, so it never skips a variable that could report.

I've put both on my fork with tests, one branch each so they can land as separate PRs if that's easier to review:

- Globals cache: https://github.com/eslint/eslint/compare/main...Cherry:eslint:perf/cache-config-globals
- `no-redeclare`: https://github.com/eslint/eslint/compare/main...Cherry:eslint:perf/no-redeclare-skip-single-declarations

### Participation

- [x] I am willing to submit a pull request for this change.

### AI acknowledgment

- [ ] I did not use AI to generate this issue report.
- [x] (If the above is not checked) I have reviewed the AI-generated content before submitting.

### Additional comments

For transparency: I used AI tooling to help profile and prototype this, and I've gone through the changes and tests myself.

The tests cover inline globals not leaking into later files that share a config, `"off"` globals staying excluded, files matching different configs keeping their own globals, and the one `no-redeclare` case where the new count and the generator differ (a config `"off"` global re-enabled inline and also declared).

Happy to adjust the approach, or split this into two issues if that's easier to track.

items.title: Bug: [prefer-arrow-callback] autofix produces a syntax error when the function is the test of a conditional

labels.name: accepted
labels.description: There is consensus among the team that this change meets the criteria for inclusion

items.body:
### Environment

Node version: v24.16.0
npm version: v11.13.0
Local ESLint version: v10.11.0 (also reproduced on main at efc4d6bd and in the playground, v10.11.0)
Global ESLint version: Not found
Operating System: darwin 24.6.0

### What parser are you using?

Default (Espree)

### What did you do?

<details>
<summary>Configuration</summary>

```js
export default [
    {
        rules: {
            "prefer-arrow-callback": "error",
        },
    },
];
```

</details>

```js
foo(function() {} ? a : b);
```

Command:

```
printf '%s' 'foo(function() {} ? a : b);' | npx eslint --no-config-lookup --rule 'prefer-arrow-callback: error' --stdin --fix-dry-run --format json
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The fix should keep the code valid by wrapping the arrow function in parentheses:

```js
foo((() => {}) ? a : b);
```

The rule already does this when the function is an operand of a logical expression. `foo(nativeCb || function() {})` becomes `foo(nativeCb || (() => {}))`.

### What actually happened?

The fixed code does not parse. Output of the command above, trimmed to `output` and `messages`:

```json
{"output": "foo(() => {} ? a : b);", "messages": [{"ruleId": null, "fatal": true, "message": "Parsing error: Unexpected token ?", "line": 1, "column": 14}]}
```

The same happens with these inputs (same command, same trimming):

```json
{"output": "foo(() => { this; } ? a : b);", "messages": [{"ruleId": null, "fatal": true, "message": "Parsing error: Unexpected token ?", "line": 1, "column": 21}]}
```

Inputs, in the same order:

- `foo(function() { this; }.bind(this) ? a : b);`
- `foo(bar ? function() {} ? a : b : c);`
- `new Foo(function() {} ? a : b);`
- `foo(async function() {} ? a : b);`

When the function is the consequent or the alternate, the output is valid: `foo(bar ? function() {} : function() {})` becomes `foo(bar ? () => {} : () => {})`.

### Additional comments

The fixer in `lib/rules/prefer-arrow-callback.js` skips the parentheses whenever the parent is a `ConditionalExpression`. That is right for the consequent and the alternate, but not for the test. An arrow function cannot be the test of `?:` without parentheses. I have a fix with tests ready: add the parentheses only when the replaced node is the `test` of the conditional.
